abstract: Cinnamon essential oil (CEO) exhibits antimicrobial activity in a dose-dependent manner, offering potential for controlling plant bacterial diseases. This study investigated the effects of CEO on Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria 173, the causal agent of pepper bacterial spot disease. Treatment with an EC50 dose of CEO significantly altered bacterial culturability and protein expression profiles. Proteomic analyses revealed that, relative to untreated control, a TonB-dependent receptor and a Clp protease were upregulated, and ATP-binding cassette transporter proteins were downregulated in the CEO-exposed X. euvesicatoria . Quantitative real-time PCR confirmed that TonB and Clp proteases abundance positively correlated with transcriptional upregulation of their corresponding genes. Our findings suggest that CEO disrupts cellular homeostasis by targeting key membrane functions. Further investigation is required to elucidate how key changes in transport and proteolytic systems contribute to the control by CEO of the plant pathogen, X. euvesicatoria .
body:
The Gram-negative bacterium
Xanthomonas euvesicatoria
pv.
euvesicatoria
is the causal agent of bacterial spot disease in pepper and tomato plants (
Osdaghi, 2022
). This pathogen causes significant economic losses with lowered harvestable yield resulting from lesion formation (
Fayette, 2010
). The pathogenic bacterium disperses in wind-driven rain droplets, enters the plant via wounds and the stomata, and proliferates in substomatal chambers and intercellular spaces. Necrotic spots result, and as the pathogen egresses from the lesions it can be disseminated to other hosts (
Potnis et al., 2015
).
Xanthomonas
infections have been controlled with copper-based bactericides. However, copper-tolerant
Xanthomonas
strains have developed as a consequence of pesticide overuse (
Obradovic et al., 2004
). The antibiotic streptomycin has also lost efficacy as some
Xanthomonas
strains have acquired resistance to it (
Potnis et al., 2015
). Recently, high biocidal activity against a
Xanthomonas
-causing leaf spot of tomato is reported for a silver-based nanocomposite. However, its efficacy under field conditions has not yet been validated (
Ocsoy et al., 2013
). Essential oils (EO) from cinnamon, citronella, cloves, eucalyptus, lemongrass, tea tree, and thyme also are directly toxic to
Xanthomonas
strains
in vitro
(
Lucas et al., 2012
).
Cinnamon (
Cinnamomum
spp.) bark and leaf extract are antibacterial (
Melo et al., 2015
), antifungal (
Wang et al., 2005
), antioxidant (
Mathew and Abraham, 2006
), nematocidal (
Kong et al., 2007
), and insecticidal (
Cheng et al., 2009
). The principal active ingredient in cinnamon EOs is cinnamaldehyde. It inhibits bacterial ATPase (
Usta et al., 2003
) and interferes with cell division in
Bacillus
spp. (
Kwon et al., 2003
). It alters cell wall biosynthesis (
OuYang et al., 2019
), and weakens membrane integrity in certain fungi (
Huang et al., 2019
).
This present study aimed to determine the effective concentrations of cinnamon essential oil (CEO) against
X. euvesicatoria
173, the causative agent of bacterial spot in pepper in South Korea (
Kyeon et al., 2016
). Proteomic changes in
X. euvesicatoria
173 exposed to a sublethal doses were examined to elucidate the mode of action of CEO.
X. euvesicatoria
pv.
euvesicatora
isolate 173 (formerly CNUPBL 2027), was obtained from Prof. Jae-Soon Cha at Chungbuk National University in South Korea (
Kyeon et al., 2016
). Bacterial cells were grown in nutrient broth consisting of 3 g/L beef extract and 5 g/L peptone in distilled water (NB, KisanBio Company, Seoul, Korea) on a shaking incubator at 150 rpm and 28°C for 48 h. Growth was monitored by measuring the OD
600
of the culture and counting the colony-forming units (CFU) on NB agar after inoculation with dilutions of the culture.
The CEO (≥97% purity) was obtained from Green Focus Co. Ltd., Asan, Korea. A 20,000-rpm stock CEO solution was prepared by dilution the concentrate with 70% alcohol (v/v). The stock CEO solution was stored in the dark at −20°C.
The chemical composition of volatiles from the CEO was determined by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS-QP NX, Shimadzu Corp., Kyoto, Japan). The GC-MS was fitted with a capillary column (No. DB-05MS, 30 cm × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm, Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). The stock CEO solution was first diluted 1,000-fold with chloroform. Volatile organic compounds were generated at an initial temperature of 100°C for 4 min. The oven temperature was increased to 130°C at a rate of 7°C per min and held there for 7 min. The injector and interface temperatures were set to 280°C and 250°C, respectively. Each 1 μL sample was injected using a 300:1 split ratio. The carrier gas was helium (He) and its flow rate was 1.2 mL/min. The MS was operated in positive electron impact mode in a scan range of
m/z
30–1,000. The ion source temperature was set to 220°C. The compounds in the CEO were identified using data from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) library (
https://www.nist.gov/nist-research-library
).
The cinnamaldehyde concentration in the CEO was quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC; SPD-M20D, Shimadzu Corp.). The device was fitted with a Capcell Pak AQ C18 UG120 column (4.6 mm I.D. × 250 mm, 5 μm, Shiseido, Tokyo, Japan). The compounds were separated by isocratic elution using HPLC-grade water containing 55:45 (v/v) 0.1% (v/v) formic acid:acetonitrile. The flow rate was 1.0 mL/min and the eluents were measured at 288 nm. The calibration curve (Y = 545,044X + 236,086;
R
2
= 0.9978) was generated using injections of defined concentrations between 1 and 40 μg of authentic cinnamaldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich Corp., St. Louis, MO, USA). Accuracy and reproducibility were evaluated by the standard spike method. Standards were added to three different CEO aliquot concentrations to determine analytical precision, and all analyses were performed in triplicate. Quantities were expressed as ratios of the peak area to the total peak area (
Table 1
,
Supplementary Fig. 1
).
Cinnamaldehyde was detected at 97% of the total relative content in the commercial preparation (
Table 1
). The remaining 3% consisted of a mixture of 2-methoxy-3-(2-propenyl) phenol (1%) and acetyl cinnamyl ester (1% cinnamyl acetate) in about equal amounts. Trace amounts of five other compounds were also detected (
Table 1
,
Supplementary Fig. 1
). The cinnamaldehyde concentrations previously reported for other commercial preparations were only in the range 60–95% (
Behbahani et al. 2020
;
El-Baroty et al. 2010
;
Valková et al., 2022
).
To determine CEO toxicity to
X. euvesicatoria
173, the stock CEO solution (20,000 ppm) was serially diluted with sterile water to concentrations ranging between 125–2,000 ppm. Ten-microliter aliquots were added to 80 μL NB in each well of a 96-well plate (SPL Life Sciences Co. Ltd., Daejeon, Korea). Each well contained 1 × 10
6
CFU/mL inoculum prepared from cells grown in 10 mL NB broth on an incubator with agitation at 150 rpm and at 28°C for 24 h. Cultures were by transferring to NB broth a single
X. euvesicatoria
173 colony grown on NB agar at 28°C for 2 days. Cells were then harvested by centrifugation, resuspended in NB broth, and 100 μL aliquots of bacterial culture transferred to the 96-well plates. Bacterial growth rates in the absence and the presence of CEO at the defined concentrations was measured in a Versa Max (Molecular Devices LLC, San Jose, CA, USA) at 48 h at OD
600
after 48 h. Responses of the bacterium to each dilution were replicated three times, and mean values were used for analysis. Growth inhibition (%) at each concentration was calculated using the formula: Inhibition (%) = [1 – (OD
600
of treatment/OD
600
of control)] × 100.
The dose-response curve was generated by plotting inhibition (%) against the logarithm of the treatment concentrations. The effective concentration 50 (EC50) and EC90 values of CEO were estimated by fitting a non-linear sigmoidal regression model (four-parameter logistic, 4PL) using GraphPad Prism (v. 10, GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA). Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was defined as the lowest concentration at which no visible bacterial growth occurred, corresponding to an OD
600
≤ 0.05 and/or is statistically equivalent to the negative control. Then 100 μL aliquots of bacterial culture were plated onto NB agar and incubated at 28°C for 24 h to determine the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC; the lowest CEO concentration killing 99.9% of all
X. euvesicatoria
cells).
Each experiment was repeated thrice, and all values were reported as means ± standard deviation. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (v. 10) and XLSTAT (Lumivero, Denver, CO, USA). Normal distribution was analyzed by the Shapiro-Wilk test. Unpaired Student’s
t
-tests, one-way analyses of variance (ANOVA) with
post hoc
multiple comparisons tests or Dunnett’s correction test and linear regressions were used to determine two-sided statistical differences between groups.
P
< 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
A non-linear sigmoidal regression model revealed that EC50 = 144 ppm, EC90 = 276 ppm, MIC = 400 ppm, and MBC = 500 ppm, respectively for 1 × 10
8
CFU/mL
X. euvesicatoria
173 (
Table 2
).
Loss of
X. euvesicatoria
culturability with exposure to CEO was evaluated by measuring CFU/mL reduction. Five-milliliter cultures were grown in NB broth for 24 h. Cells were then transferred to 150 mL fresh NB broth and grown at 28°C to the early exponential growth phase (OD
600
= 0.2). The CEO was added at the MIC or EC50 levels to 5-mL aliquots of each bacterial suspension. All samples were incubated with agitation at 150 rpm at 28°C. Bacterial suspensions were sampled after exposure to CEO for 0 h, 0.5 h, 1 h, 1.5 h, and 2 h, plated on NB agar, and the colonies enumerated. Bactericidal activity of CEO against
X. euvesicatoria
173 cultured in NB broth was time-dependent (
Fig. 1
). The MIC dose killed ~20% of all cells, while the EC50 dose also lowered cell density but to a lesser extent than the MIC dose at all time points tested (
Fig. 1
).
Changes in proteins were detected in bacteria subjected to the sublethal EC50 dose (144 ppm). Planktonic
X. euvesicatoria
173 cells were grown in NB broth with agitation at 150 rpm at 28°C for 2 days, harvested by centrifugation at 10,000 ×
g
, and resuspended in 50 mL NB broth to 1 × 10
8
CFU/mL. Half of the suspension was treated with CEO at the EC50 level, while the other was not treated. Cells were either exposed to CEO at EC50 or served as untreated controls in three independent studies. All cultures were incubated with agitation at 150 rpm and 28°C for 2 h, pelleted by centrifugation at 10,000 ×
g
. The cells were suspended in lysis buffer (8 M urea-0.1 M Tris-HCl buffer; pH 8.5) containing a protease inhibitor cocktail. The suspensions were sonicated on ice in a Covaris S2 Focused-Ultrasonicator (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA) for 20 min and centrifuged at 10,000 ×
g
for 1 h. Supernatants were collected and their protein extract concentrations were determined using a Pierce Bicinchoninic Acid Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).
The extracted protein samples were subjected to proteomic analysis performed at E-biogen Inc. (Seoul, Korea). To ensure biological reproducibility and analytical reliability, the experiment was independently performed three times. The protein extracts were passed through a Microcon 30K Centrifugal Filter Device (EMD Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA). Each 100 μg protein sample in the filtrate was reduced by incubation with 5 mM Tris (2-carboxyethyl)-phosphine (TCEP) at 37°C for 30 min and alkylated with 50 mM iodoacetic acid in the dark at 25°C for 60 min. The proteins were washed with buffer and 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and digested at 37°C with trypsin at a 1:50 (w/w) enzyme: protein ratio for 18 h. The peptide mixtures were collected in new sampling tube and the trypsin was inactivated by acidification with 15 μL formic acid (Honeywell, Charlotte, NC, USA). The peptides were desalted in C18 spin columns (Harvard Apparatus, Holliston, MA, USA) and eluted with 80% (v/v) acetonitrile in 0.1% (v/v) aqueous formic acid.
The peptides were analyzed in an UltiMate 3000 RSLC Nano LC System (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a QExactive MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The samples were passed through an Acclaim PepMap 100 Trap Column (100 mm × 2 cm, nanoViper, C18, 5 mm, 100 Å, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and separated in an Acclaim PepMap RSLC Analytical Column (75 mm × 50 cm, nanoViper, C18, 2 mm, 100 Å, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The mass spectra were acquired in data-dependent mode with an automatic switch between a full scan (m/z 400–2,000) and ten data-dependent MS/MS scans. For the full scan MS, the target value was 3,000,000, the maximum injection time was 100 ms, and the resolution was 70,000 at m/z 400. For the MS/MS, the ion target value was 100,000, the maximum injection time was 50 ms, the resolution was 17,500 at m/z 400, and the collision energy was normalized (27%). Dynamic exclusion of repeated peptides was applied for 20 s.
The MS/MS raw files for the proteins were searched with Proteome Discoverer (v. 2.5, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and the
X. euvesicatoria
database downloaded from UniProt (
https://www.uniprot.org/
). The appropriate consensus workflow included a peptide-spectrum match validation step and used the SEQUEST HT (
https://proteomicsresource.washington.edu/protocols06/sequest.php
) detection process as a database search algorithm. The search parameters were: 10 ppm precursor ion mass tolerance, 0.02 Da fragment ion mass, and a maximum of two missed trypsin cleavages. The dynamic modifications on the peptide sequence included static cysteine carbamidomethylation (+57.012 Da), variable methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da), protein
N
-terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da), and
N
-terminal protein carbamylation (+43.0006 Da). After the search, data < 1% of the false discovery rate were selected and used to filter at least six other peptide lengths.
Three independent proteomic analyses of
X. euvesicatoria
pv.
euvesicatoria
173 extracts identified and quantified 1,197 proteins in the 10–50 kDa size range. Most of them were 20–40 kDa (data not shown). Protein expression data were normalized and log
2
-transformed before statistical analysis. Differential expression was determined in triplicate for each condition by two-tailed unpaired Student’s
t
-test in GraphPad Prism v. 9 (GraphPad Software). Differentially expressed peptides (DEPs) are visualized using volcano plot analysis generated by Excel-based Differential Gene/Protein Expression Analysis (ExDEGA software version 6.0, E-biogen Inc.). Peptides were considered significantly up-regulated or down-regulated based on statistical thresholds of log
2
fold change > 1.0 or < −1.0 with a
P
< 0.05. Volcano plot analyses of the peptide expression profiles disclosed that most peptides did not significantly change in response to CEO exposure, and only a few of them underwent significant differential accumulation (
Fig. 2
). Twelve and seven peptides were significantly upregulated and downregulated, respectively. The DEPs are listed in
Table 3
and visualized in the heat map of
Fig. 3
.
To identify the metabolic and signaling pathways associated with each DEP, a Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis was conducted using the Mapper-Search Pathway tool (
https://www.genome.jp/kegg/mapper/search.html
). The DEP gene symbols were submitted to the aforementioned tool, and it mapped each gene to known KEGG pathways (
Kanehisa et al., 2015
).
The KEGG pathway enrichment analysis output was exported and is summarized in
Table 3
and
Supplementary Fig. 2
. It identified ten enriched pathways from the DEPs, and these were related to distinct metabolic and regulatory responses. Carbon metabolism, bacterial secretion system, longevity regulation pathway, β-lactam resistance, and biosynthesis of secondary metabolites were associated with upregulated peptides. Glycan degradation and the ribosome pathway were linked to downregulated peptides. As general metabolic pathways, fatty acid (FA) metabolism and ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters were related to both upregulated and downregulated peptides, indicating that these processes underwent complex modulations in response to CEO exposure.
Quantitative real time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analyses were also conducted to establish whether gene transcription is implicated in the observed responses of
X. euvesicatoria
173 to CEO. Total RNA was extracted at 60 and 120 min from xanthomonad cells exposed either to EC50 or to MIC levels of CEO in NB broth, and from untreated control cells. A Qiagen RNeasy Mini Kit and RNase-free DNase I (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) was used according to the manufacturer’s instructions to obtain the RNA. The cDNAs were generated from the RNA using a PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit (Takara Bio Inc., Kusatsu, Shiga, Japan). RT-PCR was performed using SYBR Green Premix Ex Taq II (Takara Bio Inc.) in an Applied Biosystems StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, Carlsbad, CA, USA). The gene primers were designed based on
X. euvesicatoria
50–81 genome sequences (
Supplementary Table 1
), and the transcription from the 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene was used for normalization. The primers used for the RT-PCR studies are listed in
Supplementary Table 1
. The qRT-PCR program was: 95°C for 10 min followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 5 s, 60°C for 10 s, and 72°C for 30 s. The accumulations of the transcripts were determined by the 2
−ΔΔCt
method, where ΔΔCt represents the difference in the number of threshold cycles between the target and control genes (
Liao et al., 2019
).
The PCR analysis showed that exposure to CEO upregulated expression from the gene
clpA
, encoding a subunit in the ATP-dependent Clp protease ClpX, and
tonB
, encoding a TonB-dependent receptor but to different extents and timing of exposure (
Fig. 4
). The transcription levels of
clpA
increased ~1.5-fold at 60 min and sevenfold at 120 min post-treatment. The transcription levels of
tonB
increased 3.4-fold and 20-fold at 60 min post-treatment but decreased at 120 min post-treatment. These findings correlate with the increased levels of the proteins detected at 120 min after CEO exposure revealed in the proteomics study. Further research is required to determine the dose-dependent efficacy of CEO treatments at controlling pepper bacterial spot caused by
X. euvesicatoria
.
The KEGG pathway enrichment analysis provided key insights into the molecular mechanisms affected by the CEO treatment. Exposure to the sublethal level of CEO decreased the levels of a multidrug ABC transporter, the chemotaxis protein CheY, and an acyl-CoA desaturase (
Table 3
). ABC transporters have multiple functions including regulation of cell division (
Zeng and Charkowski, 2021
) and the export of microbial pathogen virulence factors (
Akhtar and Turner, 2022
).
These findings show that the xanthomonad cells are responding with metabolic changes to CEO exposure in part conditioned by altered gene expression. Comparisons of the DEPs to results published with other phytopathogenic bacteria indicate that the changes indicate stress mitigation and altered virulence. The Clp proteases are involved in restoration of misformed proteins generated by stress. In
X. campestris
pv.
campestris
, the cause of black rot in crucifers, the Clp protease governs virulence (
Lo et al., 2020
). The subunit ClpB, which functions in another protein repair system, also enables bacteria to survive under various stress conditions. Additionally, ClpB regulates the type VI secretion system, a mechanism that transports effectors from the bacterial cytoplasm into adjacent host/target cells as part of the virulence mechanism (
Alam et al., 2021
). The TonB-dependent receptor proteins act as transporters for iron and sugars vital to
X. campestris
pv.
campestris
growth and pathogenesis (
Blanvillain et al., 2007
). The most responsive DEP, corresponding to the activity of RND pumps, suggests that the CEO-exposed cells are trying to mitigate stress by increased efflux pumping (
Huang et al., 2022
).
Other proteins were downregulated by CEO exposure: a multidrug ABC transporter, the chemotaxis regulatory protein CheY, and an acyl-CoA desaturase. These proteins play pivotal roles for bacterial cells in export and import of chemicals, environmental sensing, and membrane lipid metabolism, respectively. Our understanding of the role of the many ABC transporters in bacterial cells is limited (
Zeng and Charkowski, 2021
) and the function of the identified xanthomonad DEP is not revealed by homology to other systems. The decreased CheY abundance suggests disruption of chemotactic responses and oxidative stress regulation, which are critical for bacterial adaptation to hostile environments (
Louis et al., 2023
). The decline in acyl-CoA desaturase further implies disturbances in FA metabolism, suggesting that the cells have impacts on membrane function due to the CEO-imposed stress.
To further elucidate the precise roles of these proteins in CEO-induced stress responses and pathogenicity, we are currently constructing gene knockout mutants lacking the expression of the discrete peptides in the Clp proteases, TonB-dependent receptors, and ATP/RND exporters. These future studies will help clarify the functional significance of these pathways and support the development of targeted strategies for controlling bacterial plant pathogens using natural antimicrobial agents like CEO.
In conclusion, CEO exerts its antimicrobial effects through multifaceted mechanisms, where the genes and their proteins are involved in membrane function, detoxification pathways, and virulence factor regulation. These findings highlight the potential application of CEO as a natural, eco-friendly alternative for managing bacterial plant diseases, particularly against pathogens exhibiting chemical resistance.
